docs.title: optimized-svm
docs.text:
Support vector machines whose hyperparameters are tuned by exact gradients instead of grid search.

optimized-svm treats hyperparameter selection as a bilevel optimization problem: the upper level minimizes a (smoothed) cross-validation error, the lower level is the SVM training problem. Smoothing the loss makes the training solution differentiable in the hyperparameters, so the gradient of the CV error follows from the implicit function theorem and a quasi-Newton method (L-BFGS-B) can be used. This works for the regularization parameter and for per-feature kernel scalings (automatic relevance determination), where grid search is hopeless.

The methods are developed in

N. Strasdat, Duality, Derivative-Based Training Methods and Hyperparameter Optimization for Support Vector Machines, Dissertation, Technische Universität Dresden, 2023. urn:nbn:de:bsz:14-qucosa2-874731

Training uses the Rust SMO solver smo-solver as a warm start followed by a semismooth Newton method on the smoothed primal problem.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• scikit-learn estimators: OptimizedSVC, OptimizedSVR (tuned) and SmoothSVC, SmoothSVR (fixed hyperparameters); binary and one-vs-rest classification
  • losses: smoothed hinge, logistic (with predict_proba), smoothed ε-insensitive, squared (LS-SVM), Poisson; smoothing of degree 2, 3 or 6; sample/class weights; optional bound on Σ|α| (generalized ν-SVM)
  • exact hypergradients via one adjoint linear system per fold (verified against finite differences)
  • ARD kernels (blocks="features") with two-stage optimization, warm starts, time limits, full optimization history
  • decision_gradient() for local feature sensitivities

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install optimized-svm

For development (the solver smo-solver is installed from PyPI as a prebuilt wheel):

git clone https://github.com/wotzlaff/optimized-svm && cd optimized-svm
uv sync --group dev
uv run pytest

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVR

x, y = make_friedman1(600, noise=0.5, random_state=0)
model = OptimizedSVR(blocks="features").fit(x, y)   # one kernel scaling per feature

model.lam_            # optimized regularization parameter
model.scaling_opt_    # optimized scalings: features 5..9 (pure noise) are switched off
model.history_        # every evaluation of the CV error
model.predict(x[:5])

On a 1000-sample classification task (examples/quickstart.py) the optimizer needs 16 CV evaluations (≈10 s) versus 143 grid points (≈20 s) for GridSearchCV with sklearn.svm.SVC, with comparable test accuracy (0.844 vs. 0.856).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: step method thesis training, warm start SMO on the dual with quadratic smoothing (smo-solver) Ch. 7 training, refinement semismooth Newton on a + φ'(Ka/λ + b + sc) = 0 Ch. 8.4 CV error gradient implicit function theorem, adjoint system per fold Ch. 9.2 hyperparameter search L-BFGS-B over (log λ, log s₁, …, log s_K) Ch. 9.1, 10.4

docs.title: Reproducing the thesis
docs.text:
benchmarks/thesis_regression.py repeats the protocol of Table 10.4.1 (LIBSVM regression data, 30 random 80/20 splits, ε-SVR with cubic smoothing and LS-SVM):

python benchmarks/thesis_regression.py --datasets pyrim triazines mpg housing --splits 30

docs.title: optimized_svm.train(prob, smo_options=None, newton_options=None, alpha0=None)
docs.text:
Two-step training: SMO warm start followed by Newton refinement.

For non-smooth losses (smoothing = 0) the SMO solution is already exact; for losses without SMO formulation (squared, Poisson) Newton starts at zero.

docs.title: optimized_svm.newton(prob, a, b, c, *, tol=1e-12, max_steps=100, max_backtracks=20, sigma=0.0001, beta=0.5, verbose=0)
docs.text:
Damped semismooth Newton method for the (smoothed) primal training problem.

Requires a loss with (piecewise) second derivative. The 1-norm constraint is treated as active iff c > 0 at the starting point.

docs.title: optimized_svm.Solution dataclass
docs.text: Solution (a, b, c) of a training problem with ka = K a / lam.

docs.title: optimized_svm.losses
docs.text:
Loss functions of the training problem, expressed per loss term.

A training problem with n samples consists of m loss terms: one per sample, or two for the epsilon-insensitive loss (one for each side of the tube). Term l belongs to sample kernel_index[l], has weight w_l, label y_l and sign s_l (used by the optional 1-norm constraint, 0 if not applicable). The decision value of a term is f(x_l) + s_l c.

docs.title: Terms dataclass
docs.text: Term structure of a training problem.

docs.title: Loss
docs.text: Base class: per-term loss phi_l(t) and its derivatives.

docs.title: HingeLoss dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Loss

Smoothed hinge loss w * m_delta(shift - y t) for labels y in {-1, +1}.

docs.title: LogisticLoss dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Loss

Logistic loss w * log(1 + exp(-y t)) for y in {-1, +1} (Strasdat, Sec. 4.1.3).

Smooth without a smoothing parameter and strictly convex, but with positive curvature everywhere: the dual solution is dense and the dual is not a separable quadratic, so there is no SMO warm start and every Newton system has the full size n.

docs.title: EpsilonInsensitiveLoss dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Loss

Smoothed epsilon-insensitive loss w * (m(y - t - eps) + m(t - y - eps)).

Uses two terms per sample: sign +1 for m(y - t - eps) and -1 for the other side.

docs.title: SquaredLoss dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Loss

Least-squares loss w / 2 * (t - y)^2 (LS-SVM).

docs.title: PoissonLoss dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Loss

Poisson negative log-likelihood w * (exp(t) - y t + log(y!)) for counts y.

docs.title: ApproxPoissonLoss dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Loss

Poisson-type loss with a linear left tail (from the original experiments):

w * (exp(t) - (y + 1) t - 1 + log(y!)) for t > 0 and w * (-y t + log(y!)) else.

It is convex and continuously differentiable; for t <= 0 its curvature vanishes.

docs.title: optimized_svm.cv_error_and_gradient(theta, x, y, w, folds, loss, validation, blocks=None, max_asum=None, smo_options=None, newton_options=None, warm_start=None)
docs.text:
Mean validation error over all folds and its gradient w.r.t. theta.

warm_start is a list with one (possibly None) start vector per fold; it is updated in place with the new solutions.

docs.title: optimized_svm.fold_error_and_gradient(x_train, y_train, w_train, x_val, y_val, loss, validation, lam, blocks, max_asum=None, smo_options=None, newton_options=None, alpha0=None)
docs.text:
Validation error of one fold and its gradient w.r.t. (log lam, log s_k).

x_train/x_val must already be scaled.

docs.title: optimized_svm.validation
docs.text:
Validation error measures E(f) = sum_v L_v(f_v) for the upper level problem (Sec. 9.1.4).

All measures are differentiable so that the hyperparameter objective has a gradient.

docs.title: ValidationLoss
docs.text: Returns the summed loss and its gradient w.r.t. the predictions.

docs.title: SmoothHingeValidation dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ValidationLoss

sum_v w_v m_delta(shift - y_v f_v); balanced weights both classes equally.

docs.title: LogisticValidation dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ValidationLoss

sum_v w_v log(1 + exp(-y_v f_v)); balanced weights both classes equally.

docs.title: SmoothAbsoluteValidation dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ValidationLoss

Smoothed absolute error sum_v m_delta(f_v - y_v) + m_delta(y_v - f_v) (Huber-like).

docs.title: SquaredValidation dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ValidationLoss

1/2 sum_v (f_v - y_v)^2.

docs.title: PoissonValidation dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: ValidationLoss

Poisson deviance-type loss sum_v exp(f_v) - y_v f_v + log(y_v!).

docs.title: optimized_svm.kernels
docs.text:
Gaussian kernel with feature scaling and its derivatives w.r.t. log-scalings.

The hyperparameters of the kernel are scalings s_k > 0 of feature blocks B_k: k(x, z) = exp(-sum_k s_k^2 |x_{B_k} - z_{B_k}|^2). With a single block this is the RBF kernel with gamma = s^2; with one block per feature it is an ARD kernel. The training code works on scaled features x_{B_k} * s_k and an RBF kernel with gamma = 1.

docs.title: squared_distances(x, z)
docs.text: Matrix of squared Euclidean distances |x_i - z_j|^2 (clipped at zero).

docs.title: rbf(x, z)
docs.text: exp(-|x - z|^2) for already scaled features.

docs.title: rbf_with_gradient(x, z, blocks=None)
docs.text:
Kernel matrix and its derivatives w.r.t. the log-scalings of all blocks.

Returns K of shape (n, m) and dK of shape (n, m, n_blocks) with dK[..., k] = d K / d log s_k = -2 K * |x_{B_k} - z_{B_k}|^2 (features already scaled).

docs.title: contract_gradient(x, z, k, left, right, blocks=None)
docs.text:
Bilinear forms left^T (dK / d log s_k) right with dK_k = -2 K * |x_Bk - z_Bk|^2.

k is the kernel matrix between the (already scaled) points x and z. Same as contracting the output of :func:rbf_with_gradient, but without forming the distance matrices of the blocks: with W = K * left right^T one has sum_ij W_ij |x_i - z_j|^2 = rowsum(W) . |x|^2 + colsum(W) . |z|^2 - 2 sum(x * (W z)) per feature, so a single matrix product serves all blocks.

docs.title: scale_features(x, scaling, blocks=None)
docs.text: Multiplies the features of each block by its scaling.

docs.title: optimized_svm.smooth_max
docs.text:
Smooth approximations of the maximum function max(0, t) (Strasdat, Sec. 4.4).

Each approximation m_delta coincides with max(0, t) for |t| >= delta and is a polynomial on (-delta, delta). The degree determines the smoothness:

  • "2": C^1, piecewise quadratic (its conjugate is quadratic, so SMO applies),
  • "3": C^2, piecewise cubic,
  • "6": C^2, a single sextic polynomial on (-delta, delta).

docs.title: smooth_max(delta, degree='2')
docs.text:
Returns (m, dm, ddm): the smoothed maximum and its first two derivatives.

delta = 0 yields the (non-smooth) maximum itself.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Logistic loss (thesis Sec. 4.1.3): LogisticLoss, LogisticValidation and loss="logistic" for SmoothSVC/OptimizedSVC, including predict_proba (sigmoid of the decision values, normalised one-vs-rest probabilities for more than two classes). Trained by Newton's method only, the solution is dense; max_asum is not supported. Hypergradients are covered by the finite-difference tests.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Faster hypergradient: kernel matrices are handled per sample (ε-SVR uses n instead of 2n columns), the validation kernel columns are reused for the adjoint system, and the kernel derivatives are contracted per block with one matrix product instead of forming a distance matrix per block.
  • The Cholesky factor of the last Newton system is reused for the adjoint system when the curvature pattern is unchanged (always the case for smoothing of degree 2).
  • Linear systems of size up to 1000 are factorized with a single BLAS thread; multi-threaded LAPACK was several times slower for them, notably on shared machines. New dependency: threadpoolctl.
  • Typical effect (ε-SVR, n = 450, 5-fold, one BLAS thread): 3.2 s → 2.0 s; ARD 2.0 s → 0.9 s; classification (n = 600) 1.3 s → 0.7 s. Results are unchanged.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Warm starts were counterproductive for classification: repairing the rounding error of sum(alpha) = 0 moved a third of the variables off their bounds and made SMO take about four times as many steps as a cold start. Now about four times fewer than a cold start.

docs.title: 0.1.0 – 2026-10-28
docs.text: Complete overhaul of the 2022 code (tag legacy-2022).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• training backend: Rust solver smo-solver instead of the Nim package nimsmo
  • new package layout (src/), pyproject.toml, snake_case API, scikit-learn compatible estimators SmoothSVC, SmoothSVR, OptimizedSVC, OptimizedSVR
  • adjoint formulation of the hypergradient (one linear system per fold)

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• one-vs-rest multi-class classification, class and sample weights
  • warm starts across hyperparameter evaluations, rough SMO tolerance before Newton
  • decision_gradient() (replaces the unfinished estimate_sensitivity)
  • test suite (finite-difference checks of all gradients, scikit-learn estimator checks), documentation, examples and a reproduction script for thesis Table 10.4.1

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • see LEGACY_BUGS.md in the project workspace (P1–P13), notably: regression HPO with maxAsum did not terminate, SMO and Newton used different kernel parameters, the 1-norm constraint was always treated as active

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVC

x, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
x = StandardScaler().fit_transform(x)
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, random_state=0)

clf = OptimizedSVC(cv=5, verbose=1).fit(x_train, y_train)
print(clf.lam_, clf.scaling_opt_, clf.score(x_test, y_test))

OptimizedSVC minimizes the 5-fold cross-validation error of a smoothed hinge loss over \(\log\lambda\) and the log kernel scaling \(\log s\) (the RBF parameter is \(\gamma = s^2\)). After the search the model is refitted on all data with the best parameters.

Feature scaling

The kernel acts on the raw features. Standardize them (e.g. with StandardScaler) or use blocks="features" so that every feature gets its own scaling.

docs.title: Regression and feature relevance
docs.text:
from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVR

x, y = make_friedman1(600, noise=0.5, random_state=0)
reg = OptimizedSVR(epsilon=0.1, blocks="features").fit(x, y)
print(reg.scaling_opt_.round(3))   # small values = irrelevant features

With blocks="features" the kernel is \(k(x, z) = \exp(-\sum_j s_j^2 (x_j - z_j)^2)\). With two_stage=True (default) a single common scaling is optimized first and used as starting point.

docs.title: Choosing the model
docs.text:
estimator loss parameters SmoothSVC / OptimizedSVC (loss="hinge") smoothed hinge \(w_i\, m_\delta(\text{shift} - y_i f(x_i))\) smoothing, degree, shift, class_weight, max_asum loss="logistic" \(w_i \log(1 + e^{-y_i f(x_i)})\), enables predict_proba class_weight SmoothSVR / OptimizedSVR (loss="epsilon_insensitive") \(w_i (m_\delta(f_i - y_i - \varepsilon) + m_\delta(y_i - f_i - \varepsilon))\) epsilon, smoothing, degree loss="squared" \(\tfrac{w_i}{2} (f_i - y_i)^2\) (LS-SVM) – loss="poisson" \(w_i (e^{f_i} - y_i f_i)\), prediction \(e^{f}\) –

The logistic loss needs no smoothing, but it yields a dense solution and is trained by Newton's method only, so every training step solves a system of size \(n\): prefer the hinge loss for large \(n\) unless you need probabilities. It does not support max_asum.

smoothing (\(\delta\)) controls how strongly the kinks of the loss are rounded; degree selects the smoothing polynomial ("2": \(C^1\), exactly solvable by SMO; "3" and "6": \(C^2\)).

docs.title: Useful attributes
docs.text:
• lam_, scaling_opt_: optimized hyperparameters
  • history_: list of all CV evaluations (lam, scaling, error, gradient_norm, time, …)
  • cv_error_, time_, n_iter_
  • support_, dual_coef_, intercept_, training_info_ of the final model
  • decision_gradient(X): derivative of the decision function w.r.t. the inputs

docs.title: Lower-level building blocks
docs.text:
from optimized_svm import EpsilonInsensitiveLoss, TrainingProblem, train

prob = TrainingProblem(x * 0.5, y, EpsilonInsensitiveLoss(0.1, 0.05, "3"), lam=1e-3)
sol = train(prob)          # SMO warm start + Newton refinement
sol.a, sol.b, sol.residual

See examples/ in the repository for complete scripts.

docs.title: Reproducing the thesis
docs.text:
benchmarks/thesis_regression.py follows the protocol of Sec. 10.4.2:

  • LIBSVM regression datasets (downloaded and cached on first use),
  • 30 random splits, 80 % for hyperparameter optimization and training, 20 % for testing,
  • features and targets standardized on the training part,
  • smoothed \(\varepsilon\)-SVR with cubic smoothing (\(\delta = \varepsilon/4\)) for \(\varepsilon \in \{0.1, 0.25, 0.5\}\) and the LS-SVM,
  • 5-fold CV with the smoothed absolute validation error (\(\delta = 0.1\)),
  • start \(\lambda = 10^{-2}\), \(\gamma = \log 2 / d\); bounds \(\lambda \in [10^{-6}, 1]\), \(\gamma \in [10^{-12}, 10^4]\); time limit 600 s,
  • datasets with more than 1000 samples are subsampled to 1000.
python benchmarks/thesis_regression.py --splits 30

docs.title: Diagnosis of the mpg/housing deviation
docs.text:
• Not the optimizer. A dense GridSearchCV over (C, γ) (SVR) or KernelRidge (LS-SVM) with the same standardization and CV reaches the same test error on the same 30 splits: mpg 7.84 ± 0.36 (SVR grid) and 7.51 (LS-SVM, identical to ours); housing 10.9 (LS-SVM grid, ours 10.85). The gradient method therefore does not get stuck in a poor local minimum, and for the LS-SVM the implementation agrees with an independent solver.
  • Split noise contributes but does not explain it alone. The per-split MSE of mpg has a standard deviation of about 2; the mean over 30 splits varies by roughly ±0.4. For mpg the thesis value lies about 2 standard errors below ours, but housing deviates in the same direction.
  • Binarising nominal features does not help. The OpenML versions of the data sets (autoMpg, id 196; boston, id 531) have nominal columns (mpg: cylinders, model, origin; housing: CHAS, RAD). One-hot encoding them (mpg: 7 → 25 columns, housing: 13 → 22) makes the results worse (mpg LS-SVM 7.96, housing LS-SVM 11.54).

  • Different protocols are not comparable. The 2018/19 runs of hpo4svm on OpenML use the 10-fold CV of the OpenML tasks (3/5/10 inner folds). A 10-fold CV of a KernelRidge grid on the LIBSVM data gives MAE 1.87 (mpg) and 2.09 (housing), close to our values.

  • The old code does not reproduce the splits. The 2018/19 prototype hpo4svm draws its splits with np.random.seed(42) and np.random.permutation; replaying that sequence on the LIBSVM files (datasets in the order pyrim, triazines, mpg, housing) does not reproduce Table 10.4.1 (pyrim LS-SVM MSE 0.0100 instead of 0.0060, mpg 8.37 instead of 6.63). That script is a later experiment (3-fold CV, different bounds); the script that produced the table and the input files (~/daten/regression/<name>/data.mat) are not available.

The cause of the deviation remains open. Remaining candidates are the exact data set versions and preprocessing used in the thesis (not documented there; the protocol is adopted from Fischer et al., Optim. Methods Softw. 30(6), 2015) and the specific random splits.

docs.title: Class probabilities with the logistic loss¶
docs.text:
loss="logistic" trains the SVM with the logistic loss of the thesis (Sec. 4.1.3) and enables predict_proba. We tune it with OptimizedSVC and compare it with the smoothed hinge loss, whose decision values we pass through a sigmoid for the comparison.

The logistic loss needs no SMO warm start and gives a dense solution, so every Newton system has the full size n: it is the slower of the two and meant for moderate n.

docs.title: Quickstart: gradient-based tuning vs. grid search¶
docs.text: OptimizedSVC tunes the regularisation lam and the kernel scaling by minimising the cross-validation error with exact gradients. We compare it with GridSearchCV on a noisy classification task.

docs.title: Bilevel formulation
docs.text:
Let \(\theta = (\log\lambda, \log s_1, \dots, \log s_K)\) collect the hyperparameters. For folds \((T_j, V_j)\) the upper level problem is

\[ \min_\theta\; E(\theta) = \frac{1}{|V|}\sum_j \sum_{v \in V_j} L\big(f_j(x_v; \theta), y_v\big), \]

where \(f_j\) is the decision function trained on \(T_j\) (the lower level problem) and \(L\) a smooth validation loss: a smoothed hinge for classification, a Huber-type smoothed absolute error, the squared error or the Poisson loss for regression (Sec. 9.1).

docs.title: Implicit function theorem
docs.text:
With smoothed losses, the training solution satisfies the (semismooth) optimality system

\[ a_l + \phi_l'(\mathrm{ka}_l + b + s_l c) = 0, \qquad \mathbf 1^\top a = 0, \qquad (s^\top a = A), \]

with \(\mathrm{ka} = K a/\lambda\). Only terms \(P = \{l : \phi_l'' > 0\}\) react to small changes of \(\theta\); all others keep \(a_l\) constant. Differentiating the system on \(P\) gives (Sec. 9.2)

\[ \begin{pmatrix} K_{PP}/\lambda + \operatorname{diag}(1/h_P) & \mathbf 1 & s_P\\ \mathbf 1^\top & 0 & 0\\ s_P^\top & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\partial a_P\\ \partial b\\ \partial c\end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix}\partial_\theta \mathrm{ka}_P\\ 0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad h = \phi''. \]

docs.title: Adjoint system
docs.text:
Instead of solving this system for every hyperparameter, the chain rule is applied in reverse: one solves the transposed (symmetric) system with right-hand side \((K_{VP}^ op abla L/\lambda,\; \mathbf 1^ op abla L,\; 0)\) for \(u\) and obtains

\[ rac{\partial E}{\partial heta} = -u^ op \partial_ heta \mathrm{ka}_P + abla L^ op \partial_ heta f_V ig|_{a\ ext{fixed}}, \]

with \(\partial_{\log\lambda}\mathrm{ka} = -\mathrm{ka}\) and \(\partial_{\log s_k} K = -2 K \odot D_k\) (\(D_k\): squared distances in block \(k\) of the scaled features). The cost per fold is one factorization of a matrix of size \(|P|\), independent of the number of hyperparameters — this is what makes ARD kernels affordable. For the quadratic smoothing \(h\) is piecewise constant, so the Newton system of the last training step has the same matrix as the adjoint system and its Cholesky factor is reused; for other degrees the matrix is factorized again. Contractions with \(\partial_{\log s_k} K\) do not form the matrices \(D_k\): \(\sum_{ij} W_{ij}\lVert x_{i,B_k} - z_{j,B_k} Vert^2\) is evaluated from row and column sums of \(W\) and one product \(WZ\) for all blocks.

The implementation is tested against central finite differences for all losses, smoothing degrees, ARD blocks and an active \( u\)-constraint (relative error about \(10^{-8}\)).

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text: L-BFGS-B runs on \(\theta\) within box constraints. Each evaluation warm-starts SMO with the fold solutions of the previous evaluation (about ten times fewer SMO steps for regression). With time_limit, the best parameters found so far are used.

docs.title: Standard training problem
docs.text:
For samples \((x_i, y_i)\), a feature map \(\varphi\) with kernel \(k(x, z) = \langle\varphi(x),\varphi(z)\rangle\) and convex losses \(\ell_i\), the standard training problem (Strasdat, Def. 2.5) reads

\[ \min_{w, b}\; \frac{\lambda}{2}\|w\|^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\langle w, \varphi(x_i)\rangle + b). \]

Its Fenchel dual is (Cor. 3.11)

\[ \min_{\alpha}\; \frac{1}{2\lambda}\alpha^\top K \alpha + \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i^\star(-\alpha_i) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \mathbf 1^\top\alpha = 0, \]

and \(w = \frac1\lambda \sum_i \alpha_i \varphi(x_i)\) (representer theorem). The decision function is \(f(x) = \frac1\lambda\sum_i \alpha_i k(x, x_i) + b\).

docs.title: Smoothed losses
docs.text:
Hinge and \(\varepsilon\)-insensitive losses are built from \(\max(0, t)\). Replacing it by a smooth approximation \(m_\delta\) that agrees with \(\max(0, t)\) for \(|t| \ge \delta\) (Sec. 4.4) yields differentiable losses. For the quadratic smoothing

\[ m_\delta(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & t \le -\delta\\ \frac{(t+\delta)^2}{4\delta} & |t| < \delta \\ t & t \ge \delta\end{cases} \]

the conjugate is quadratic on an interval, so the dual is still a box-constrained QP that SMO solves exactly. The higher degree variants ("3", "6") are \(C^2\).

docs.title: Two-step training
docs.text:
1. SMO (smo-solver) solves the dual with quadratic smoothing to a rough tolerance (Ch. 7). Working set selection uses second-order information and shrinking removes variables fixed at their bounds.
  2. Semismooth Newton (Ch. 8.4) solves the optimality system of the actual (possibly higher-degree) smoothed problem

$$ a + \ell'(\tfrac1\lambda K a + b\mathbf 1 + s c) = 0, \qquad \mathbf 1^\top a = 0 $$

Terms with vanishing curvature (\(\ell'' = 0\)) are fixed explicitly, so only a linear system on the terms with \(\ell'' > 0\) has to be solved. Usually one to a few steps suffice.

For non-smooth losses (\(\delta = 0\)) only SMO is used; for losses without an SMO formulation (squared, logistic, Poisson) Newton starts at zero.

docs.title: Logistic loss
docs.text: The logistic loss \(\ell(t) = \log(1 + e^{-yt})\) (Sec. 4.1.3) is smooth without any smoothing and its curvature \(\ell''(t) = \sigma(-yt)\,\sigma(yt)\) is positive everywhere. Its conjugate involves \(x \log x\) (an entropy), so the dual is not a separable quadratic and SMO cannot be used. Newton's method works as usual (about 5–9 steps from zero), but because no term has vanishing curvature the solution is dense and every Newton system has the full size \(n\) (cost \(\mathcal O(n^3)\) per step). In exchange the decision values have a probabilistic reading, \(P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(f(x))\), used by predict_proba. On the checkerboard-like test sets of the benchmarks its accuracy matches the smoothed hinge loss, the test log-loss is slightly better, and training is 3–6 times slower at \(n = 2000\). Starting Newton at the solution of neighbouring hyperparameters does not help: the dual coefficients \(a = -\ell'(f)\) change with the kernel, so the previous \(a\) is no better than zero.

docs.title: Optional 1-norm constraint
docs.text: max_asum=A adds \(\sum_i |\alpha_i| \le A\) (a generalized \(\nu\)-SVM, Sec. 5.2). Its multiplier \(c \ge 0\) shifts the decision values of the training terms by \(s_i c\).
